title: Puppy Blues: Feeling Regret After Getting a Puppy (and What Helps)
description: Feeling regret or overwhelm after getting a puppy? Learn what puppy blues are, why they happen, what usually helps and when to ask for support.
excerpt: Feeling tired, anxious or regretful after getting a puppy is common. Here is what research says and what helps.
seoTitle: Puppy Blues: Regret After Getting a Puppy and What Helps
imageAlt: Golden retriever puppy on a dark floor looking at the camera
html:
If you brought home a puppy and feel more exhausted, anxious or tearful than excited, you are not alone, and it does not mean you made a terrible mistake. This pattern is common enough that researchers have studied it and given it a name: the “puppy blues”.

This article explains what puppy blues are, why they happen, what usually helps, and when it is worth asking a professional for support.

What are the puppy blues?

Puppy blues describe the low, anxious or overwhelmed feelings some people have in the first weeks or months after getting a puppy. Many compare it to the “baby blues” new parents describe: you love the little one, and you are also worn out and unsure you are doing it right.

A 2024 study from the University of Helsinki, published in npj Mental Health Research, built the first questionnaire to measure it. The researchers collected answers from about 1,800 dog owners, most of them in Finland. Just under half of the owners reported significant negative experiences during their dog's puppyhood, and only around one in ten reported the most severe level of strain. The study also found the feelings tend to fade relatively quickly.

The same research described three main parts of the experience:

  • Anxiety: worrying that you are doing something wrong or that something bad will happen.
  • Frustration: feeling irritated by the biting, accidents or constant demands.
  • Weariness: being tired in a way that makes everything feel heavier.

Keep in mind the limits: most participants were Finnish and most were women, so the exact percentages may not match every country. The main message still applies. Feeling this way is common and it is usually temporary.

Why a puppy can feel so hard

A puppy changes your day almost overnight. The things that most often wear people down are simple and very practical:

  • Broken sleep. Young puppies cannot hold their bladder all night, so night-time trips outside and crying are normal. See what to check when a puppy cries at night.
  • Constant supervision. A puppy cannot be left to roam, so you rarely get a true break.
  • Biting and chewing. Sharp teeth on hands and ankles are normal, but painful. Our guide to stopping puppy biting covers a calm method.
  • Potty accidents. Progress is rarely a straight line. A simple daily potty schedule helps.
  • Too much conflicting advice. Every video and forum says something different, which makes it easy to feel you are failing.

The related research found puppy blues are more common among people who are younger, have less experience with dogs, have no children, or are going through other stressful life events. If that sounds like you, that is a reason to be gentle with yourself, not a sign you are unsuited to having a dog.

What usually helps

None of these steps will fix everything in a day. Small changes tend to help most.

  1. Lower the bar for now. The first weeks are for survival and routine, not perfection. A spotless house and a perfectly trained puppy are not the goal yet.
  2. Pick one routine and repeat it. Meals, outings, naps and bedtime at roughly the same times make a puppy more predictable. A predictable puppy is easier to live with.
  3. Protect your sleep where you can. If someone else lives with you, take turns with the night shift. If you are on your own, ask a friend or family member to cover one morning so you can rest.
  4. Plan breaks. Use a safe space such as a crate or playpen so your puppy rests while you step away for a few minutes. Puppies need many naps, and so do you.
  5. Use one trusted source of advice. Your veterinarian, a qualified positive-reinforcement trainer, or a puppy class is better than scrolling through ten opinions.
  6. Tell someone how you feel. Saying “this is harder than I expected” to a friend, or to other puppy owners, often makes it feel lighter.

A simple first-week plan to feel more in control

If you are overwhelmed right now, try this for seven days before judging how things are going:

  • Write down a daily rhythm with set meal, outing, nap and bedtime slots.
  • Take your puppy out after waking, after eating and after play, and reward calmly when they go outside.
  • Offer a chew toy when the biting starts, and give yourself a short pause when it gets too much.
  • Book a first veterinary visit if you have not already, and bring your questions.
  • Choose one thing to improve each day, not ten.

Our free New Puppy Survival Guide includes checklists, routines and a 14-day plan if you want the whole structure in one place.

When to ask for more help

Puppy blues usually ease as your puppy grows and your routine settles. Reach out to a professional if:

  • The low mood, hopelessness or anxiety lasts for weeks and does not improve, or begins to affect your work, relationships or daily life.
  • You have thoughts of harming yourself. In that case, contact local emergency services or a crisis line in your country right away.
  • You feel unsafe around your puppy or are worried you might hurt it. Ask a veterinarian or qualified trainer for urgent guidance.
  • Your puppy has behavior that worries you, such as aggression, severe fear or signs of illness. Talk to your veterinarian first.

A doctor or a mental health professional can help with the way you feel. A veterinarian or qualified trainer can help with the puppy. Asking for help is a sign you take both seriously.

Is it normal to wonder if you made a mistake?

Yes. Many people have that thought in the hardest weeks, and it does not make you a bad owner. For most people the feeling passes as sleep returns and the puppy learns the routine. If it does not pass, or if you truly cannot give your puppy a safe home, talk with your veterinarian, the breeder or shelter you got your puppy from, or a local rescue about the options. Making that call thoughtfully is better than staying silent.

Source: University of Helsinki research team, development and validation of a puppy blues scale, npj Mental Health Research (2024), DOI 10.1038/s44184-024-00072-z. This article is general information and does not replace advice from a veterinarian, a trainer or a mental health professional.
